summary.text: 地 means “earth” or “ground,” and can also mean land, territory, or place. Its received analysis combines 土, which supplies the earth-related meaning category, with 也 as a sound component.

formation.text: 地 is analyzed as a phonosemantic compound: 土 contributes an earth-related meaning category, and 也 supplies a sound cue. This is an explicit Han-period analysis, though it does not settle how the earliest graph was formed.

components.text: 土 is the left component in the received analysis and contributes the earth-related meaning category.

也 is the right component in the received analysis and serves as a phonetic component. Zhengzhang Old Chinese reconstructions are approximately related, though modern Mandarin 地 dì and 也 yě differ. This supports a sound role but does not prove the graph’s original design. The original referent of 也 is unsettled, so it is not treated as a picture within 地.

sound_limitation.text: The comparison is reconstructed rather than directly recorded, and does not by itself prove the graph’s original design rationale.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang Old Chinese, the reconstructions are approximately related; in modern Mandarin, 地 dì and 也 yě differ.

history.text: A cataloged Western Zhou bronze form has a complex right element identified as 它 in one account. The Shuowen seal-script form has 土 on the left and 也 on the right. The proposal that 它 was later regularized as 也 is an interpretation, not a change established by the forms alone.

地 is also discussed alongside 墬. One proposal treats 墬 as an earlier graph for the earth sense, but the relationship could instead involve parallel or replaced graph use; its chronology is unresolved.

uncertainties.text: The received 土-plus-也 analysis is explicit, but earlier forms have competing interpretations. The proposed 它-to-也 graphic history and the graph’s earliest design remain uncertain.

senses.text: The earliest inspectable account here describes 地 as the heavy, turbid yin counterpart to heaven and as the place where things are arrayed. This attested account does not establish the word’s hypothetical original meaning.
Cited texts show noun uses for ground, cultivated land, territory, place, and region. They do not establish when each sense first arose or a complete sequence of change.

senses.gloss: grammatical particle after an adjective, commonly read de
senses.period: Song citation; exact first use unresolved
senses.text: A Song text is cited for 地 following an adjective. This attests the use in that textual tradition, but does not show how it arose from the noun or another form.

senses.period: Yuan citation; exact first use unresolved
senses.text: A Yuan text is cited for a postverbal use glossed as ‘stand there/remain’; its precise relation to other uses of 地 is unclear.

developments.text: Earth or ground and land or territory are documented noun uses, but the stages and dates linking them are unresolved.

One proposal derives the manner particle through a path from “an adjective place” to “in an adjective manner.” Other analyses connect it to 的 or to demonstrative or interrogative forms. No single derivation or full sequence is established.

limitations.text: Citations to classical works do not independently date surviving wording. The earliest attestations and semantic links among noun senses remain unresolved.
The particle’s relation to the noun 地, to 的, or to demonstrative or interrogative forms remains disputed; no single historical pathway is established.

components.text: 土 points to the character’s earth-related meaning.

takeaway.text: 地 also follows adjectives as a particle, but how that use relates to the earth-and-ground noun remains disputed.

items.period: Late Western Zhou, associated with 㝬簋
items.caption: A bronze-script form consists of a tall, branching left element beside a more complex right element. The catalog identifies the latter in early forms as 它, while the later Shuowen analysis identifies 也 as the phonetic; this reading of the change is reported, not independently established by the drawing alone.
items.alt: Black drawing of a bronze-script glyph: a tall branching form on the left and a larger, curved, multi-part form on the right.
items.selection_reason: Shows the early form cited in a competing account of the phonetic element, useful for explaining why the received 土-plus-也 analysis does not settle the graph’s earlier components.
items.rights: CC0 1.0, as stated on the Commons page for the representation and its cited Xiaoxuetang source image.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script tradition; dictionary compiled in the Eastern Han (c. 100 CE)
items.caption: The seal-script form has 土 on the left and a rounded, vertically divided element on the right. Shuowen analyzes 地 as 从土也聲, assigning 土 the meaning and 也 the sound; the drawing illustrates that transmitted analysis but does not establish the graph’s earliest design.
items.alt: Black seal-script drawing with a tall left element and a rounded, vertically divided right element.
items.selection_reason: Pairs a visibly different transmitted form with Shuowen’s explicit component analysis, helping explain the established lexicographic account alongside uncertainty about earlier forms.
items.rights: CC0 1.0, as stated on the Commons page; the specific Sinica image is also identified there as CC0.

limitations.text: The bronze form is a modern redraw tied by its catalog description to a late Western Zhou record. Its components and reading have not been independently established from an inspected inscription; the catalog’s 它-to-也 account remains a reported interpretation.

Shuowen’s 土-plus-也 analysis is an Eastern Han lexicographic account, not direct proof of the graph’s earliest design. The relation between 地 and the related form 墬 is also not securely established as chronological ancestry.
